A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LINGOLY-TOO and the same underlying 82 UKLO problems. Their text, figures, tables, mathematical examples and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganisation.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, fine-tuning and tokenisation experiments, and a randomised study with 172 human participants.

after.justification: V4 retains original model and human results and reports additional compute-setting comparisons, expert-guidance results and reasoning-trace observations.

M1.justification: The proposed annotation, ruleset sampling and grapheme-substitution procedure remains unchanged, including sets, tables, free-tables and fixed graphemes. V1 Appendix C matches v4 Appendix B. The reasoning-equivariant terminology and additional evaluation treatments do not establish a redesigned benchmark-generation method.

E1.justification: V4 adds a limited assisted-reasoning scenario in which models receive expert-written solution steps for Problems 69 and 164, changing the information available to the solver. The underlying 82 UKLO problems, linguistic domains, difficulty levels and six-problem human study remain the same.

E2.justification: V4 retains the 11 main comparison entries and adds Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 without thinking and o3-mini low. Existing Claude 3.7 and o3-mini entries correspond to the later thinking and high settings. The separate base/fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B/3B comparisons disappear.

E3.justification: V4 introduces worst-permutation scoring, explicit thinking/compute controls and difficulty-stratified resourcedness regressions instead of v1's pooled regressions. The fine-tuning split protocol and standalone CoT test disappear. Its 6,995-pair description corrects v1's conflicting main-text count; v1 Table 7 already reports 6,995, so an actual reduction or rerun is not established.

E4.justification: V4 adds expert-guidance testing, manual reasoning-trace cases, compute-setting comparisons and LLM results alongside the six human-study problems. It revises the resourcedness analysis to account for difficulty. V1's fine-tuning generalisation study, CoT prompting check and linguistic-subdiscipline validation are removed, substantially changing the supporting analyses.

E5.justification: V4 newly displays standard errors in Figure 2 and Table 1 and 95% regression confidence bands in Figure 5. It removes v1 Appendix K.2's human-study interval based on 10,000 bootstrap samples. The 500-sample benchmark bootstrap and principal human statistical tests remain; additional independent model runs are not established.

E6.justification: New results include robust scores, Claude 3.7 thinking versus non-thinking performance of 43% versus 30%, and expert-guidance performance increasing from 66% to 76%. V4 Table 10 adds LLM results alongside retained human scores. Fine-tuning and CoT results disappear. A retained response-count entry also changes: GPT-4o empty responses are 176 in v1 Table 7 and 55 in v4 Table 6.

T1.justification: V4 Section 3.4 introduces the mathematical definition of M_obf (Robust), taking the minimum score across a question's permutations. The structured-permutation definitions, combinatorial counts and linguistic derivations in the ruleset appendix remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: V4 makes ITC models' relative progress and greater reasoning consistency central abstract, introduction and conclusion claims. It drops v1's conclusion about simple fine-tuning failing to produce robust problem solving and refocuses the contribution on separating inductive reasoning from internalised knowledge, beyond the earlier contamination emphasis.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations connecting ITC success to transfer from mathematical/coding reasoning and expert guidance to improved test-time induction. Its limitations replace the lack-of-model-improvement discussion with reasoning-domain and modality boundaries. V1's fine-tuning overfitting interpretation and subdiscipline-specific exposure explanation disappear. The human-study unfamiliarity caveat remains.

D1.justification: V4 adds a Hugging Face access pointer, dataset archive and licensing/gating metadata, four-GPU node details, participant instructions and previously redacted ethics information. These mainly expand disclosure for retained work. Fine-tuning hyperparameters, checkpoint promises and the CoT prompt are removed with their experiments.

R1.justification: V4 adds references including BIG-Bench Extra Hard, Humanity's Last Exam and the ARC Prize 2024 report, while omitting Linguini, PuzzLing Machines and parts of the earlier CoT/dual-process literature. Emphasis shifts toward ITC and reasoning-estimate validity, but the central positioning through LINGOLY and template-based perturbation remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before the benchmark, a separate Discussion section appears, validation is reorganised, and annotation/ruleset appendices exchange order. Terminology shifts systematically toward permutations and internalised knowledge.

P2.justification: V4 changes the main text from two columns to one and redraws Figure 1. Figure 2 gains robust scores, error bars and a difficulty heatmap; the earlier permutation heatmap moves to Figure 4. Resourcedness plots are redesigned, tables are restructured, several analysis displays disappear, and participant-instruction screenshots are added.

improvement.justification: V4 modestly strengthens the central evaluation through worst-permutation scoring, explicit compute comparisons and difficulty-controlled resourcedness analysis, while clarifying benchmark counts and access. These gains are tempered by losing v1's fine-tuning, CoT and subdiscipline checks and human bootstrap interval. The new guidance evidence covers only two problems, and v4's no-context prose reverses Table 1's aggregate model-score assignments. Overall, measurement and usability improve, but the evidential gains remain limited.
